newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croats see currency movements aiding tourism.
newsitem.headline: Croats see currency movements aiding tourism.

text.p: Croatian hoteliers hope for a boost in trade this year from foreign tourists because of the stronger Italian lira and weaker German mark, according to Croatian monthly business magazine Banka.
Foreign visitors are seen as vital to better tourism earnings, as many Croats go to their own cottages and spend only marginally more on holiday than they would at home.
This coming season is expected to mark the full return of Croatia to the maps of tour operators after its flagship trade languished because of conflicts in former Yugoslavia.
Leading operators put Croatian destinations in their brochures again this year after leaving them out since the 1991 outbreak of war in former Yugoslavia.
Among them are British Thompson and Germany's TUI and Neckermann that together control a half of the European travel market, Banka said.
If predictions about a return of foreigners come true, it may be a chance for some hoteliers particularly on the southern Dalmatian coast to recover from earlier losses.
They have invested heavily in refurbishing hotel rooms, camps and other facilities in preparation for it.
A recent decline of the mark against the dollar has made distant travel too expensive for Germans, making them opt for closer destinations instead, Banka said.

Judging by the bookings, they have seen the advantage of Croatia over its Adriatic neighbour Italy because of the firming lira, it quoted Franko Palma, director of hotel firm Riviera from Porec on the Istrian peninsula, as saying.
On the other hand, the lira's strength should in turn spur more business from Italians, said another hotelier.
Germans and Italians are reportedly the best spenders of all tourists, who also include Austrians, Britons and Dutch.
But hoteliers are also looking to Slovenes and tourists from the former Eastern bloc countries to help occupancy up in early and late summer.

Tourism Minister Niko Bulic forecast this year's earnings at between 13 and 14 billion kuna ($2.1-$2.3 billion) after a projected rise of 30-40 percent from 1996 -- the first year of recovery after trade slumped during the 1991-95 Balkan war.
He estimated total overnights at over 26.5 million, topping last year's by 20 percent.
